questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

The new guidelines regarding safety protocols (1)/ issued last month by the department (2)/ has not yet been implemented at the local units (3)/ despite repeated notices. (4)

options.text: The new guidelines regarding safety protocols (1)
issued last month by the department (2)
has not yet been implemented at the local units (3)

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error is in **part (3)** of the sentence due to a **subject-verb agreement** issue.
 
• The main subject of the sentence is "**The new guidelines**," which is **plural**.
 
• According to the rules of subject-verb agreement, a plural subject must be paired with a plural verb. Therefore, the singular verb "**has**" should be replaced by the plural verb "**have**."
 
• The phrase "regarding safety protocols issued last month by the department" is a descriptive phrase modifying the subject and does not change the subject's number.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The new guidelines regarding safety protocols issued last month by the department **have** not yet been implemented at the local units despite repeated notices."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(1): "The new guidelines regarding safety protocols"** – This part is correct; "regarding" is used as a preposition meaning "about."
 
• **(2): "issued last month by the department"** – This is a reduced relative clause (which were issued...) and is grammatically sound.
 
• **(4): "despite repeated notices."** – This part is correct; "despite" is a preposition followed by a noun phrase, correctly showing contrast.
 
• **Tip:** To find the subject in long sentences, ignore the phrases between the main noun and the verb (e.g., "The guidelines... have...").

questions.question:
Change the following from active to passive:

The team has finished the project two days before the deadline.

options.text: The project is finished two days before the deadline by the team.
The project has been finished two days before the deadline by the team.
The team was finished the project two days before the deadline.
The project were finished two days before the deadline by the team.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Passive voice structure: To convert a sentence from active to passive voice, the object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence.
 
• Identify the tense: The original sentence "The team has finished the project..." uses the **Present Perfect** tense (has + past participle).
 
• Conversion rule: In the Present Perfect tense, the passive structure is **"Subject + has/have + been + past participle + by + agent."**
 
• Applying the rule: "The project" (singular subject) + "has been" + "finished" + "by the team" + "two days before the deadline."

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The project has been finished two days before the deadline by the team."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: **"The project is finished..." – This is the Present Simple Passive form.
 
• **Option 3: **"The team was finished..." – This is grammatically incorrect as it implies the team itself was the thing being finished.
 
• **Option 4: **"The project were finished..." – This is incorrect because "were" is plural, but "project" is singular, and it uses the Past Simple tense.

questions.question:
Change the following from active to passive:

Scientists are developing a new vaccine to combat the rapidly mutating virus.

options.text: A new vaccine is being developed by scientists to combat the rapidly mutating virus.
A new vaccine has been developed by scientists.
The rapidly mutating virus is being combated by a new vaccine.
Scientists had developed a new vaccine to combat the virus.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Passive voice structure: To convert to passive voice, the object of the active sentence ("a new vaccine") becomes the subject of the passive sentence.
 
• Identify the tense: The original sentence "Scientists are developing..." is in the **Present Continuous** tense.
 
• Conversion rule: For the Present Continuous tense, the passive structure is **"Subject + is/am/are + being + past participle + by + agent."**
 
• Applying the rule: "A new vaccine" (singular subject) + "is being" + "developed" (past participle) + "by scientists."
 
• The infinitive phrase "to combat the rapidly mutating virus" remains attached to the action for clarity.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"A new vaccine is being developed by scientists to combat the rapidly mutating virus."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: **"A new vaccine has been developed..." – Incorrect tense (Present Perfect Passive).
 
• **Option 3: **"The rapidly mutating virus is being combated..." – Changes the primary object of the sentence; the original focus was on developing the vaccine.
 
• **Option 4: **"Scientists had developed..." – Incorrect tense (Past Perfect) and remains in the active voice.

questions.question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

She said, "Are you coming to the party?"

options.text: She asked whether I was coming to the party.
She asked if I have been coming to the party.
She asked was I coming to the party.
She asked that I come to the party.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Direct Speech:** She said, "Are you coming to the party?"
 
• **Key Conversions:**
 
 
• **Reporting Verb:**
 
 
• Since the direct speech is a question, the reporting verb "said" is changed to **"asked"**, "enquired", or "wondered".
 
 
 
• **Connectors (If/Whether):**
 
 
• For Yes/No questions (questions starting with auxiliary verbs like 'Are', 'Is', 'Do'), the conjunction **"if"** or **"whether"** is used to introduce the reported speech.
 
 
 
• **Tense Shift (Present Continuous to Past Continuous):**
 
 
• The Present Continuous tense **"Are you coming"** backshifts to the Past Continuous tense **"was coming"** in indirect speech.
 
 
 
• **Sentence Structure:**
 
 
• The interrogative form (Verb + Subject) changes to the assertive form (Subject + Verb). Thus, "Are you..." becomes **"I was..."**.
 
 
 
• **Pronoun Change:**
 
 
• The pronoun **"you"** (second person) changes according to the object of the reporting verb (which is implied as 'me' here), thus becoming **"I"**.
 
 
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"She asked whether I was coming to the party."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2:** Uses the Present Perfect Continuous tense ("have been coming"), which is an incorrect tense conversion for the Present Continuous.
 
• **Option 3:** Incorrectly maintains the interrogative word order ("was I") instead of the required assertive word order ("I was").
 
• **Option 4:** Changes the nature of the sentence from a question to a request or statement using "that," which is grammatically incorrect for reporting a Yes/No question.

questions.question:
Change the voice of the following sentence.

Please let all the rubbish be cleared immediately from this place and the furniture be brought from the next room.

options.text: Please clear all the rubbish from this place immediately from the next room and bring the furniture.
Please clear all the rubbish from this place immediately and the furniture be brought from the next room.
Please clear all the rubbish from this place immediately and bring the furniture into the next room.
Please clear all the rubbish from this place immediately and bring the furniture from the next room.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Passive to Active (Imperative):** The original sentence is in the passive voice using the "Let + Object + be + Past Participle" structure for polite commands or requests.
 
• To convert this to the active voice, we remove the "let" and "be" and use the base form of the verb directly as an imperative: **"Verb + Object."**
 
• **First part:** "Please let all the rubbish be cleared..." becomes "Please clear all the rubbish..."
 
• **Second part:** "...and the furniture be brought..." becomes "...and bring the furniture..."
 
• The word **"Please"** is retained to maintain the polite tone of the request.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Please clear all the rubbish from this place immediately and bring the furniture from the next room."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: **"Please clear all the rubbish from this place immediately from the next room..." – This incorrectly links the "next room" to the rubbish instead of the furniture.
 
• **Option 2: **"...and the furniture be brought..." – The second half of this sentence remains in the passive voice.
 
• **Option 3: **"...bring the furniture **into** the next room." – This changes the preposition and thus the meaning of the sentence (moving furniture *to* rather than *from*).

questions.question:
Transform the following sentence into active voice.

Din-i-Ilahi was a religion which was propounded by Akbar the Great.

options.text: Din-i-Ilahi was a religion which Akbar the Great propounded.
Din-i-Ilahi was a religion which did Akbar the Great propound.
Din-i-Ilahi was a religion which did Akbar the Great propounded.
Din-i-Ilahi had been a religion which Akbar the Great propounded.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Voice in Relative Clauses:** In the original sentence, the main clause "Din-i-Ilahi was a religion" is a statement of fact using a linking verb. The relative clause "which **was propounded** by Akbar the Great" is in the **Passive Voice**.
 
• **Identify the Tense:** "Was propounded" is the **Simple Past Passive**. When converting to active voice, the verb should change to the **Simple Past Active** form: "propounded."
 
• **Identify the Agent:** The agent (the person doing the action) is "Akbar the Great." In the active voice, this agent becomes the subject of the relative clause.
 
• **Restructure:** The relative pronoun "which" remains the object of the clause, but the structure shifts to **"Subject + Verb + Object"** (Akbar the Great propounded which/it).

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Din-i-Ilahi was a religion which Akbar the Great propounded."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: **"...which did Akbar the Great propound." – Using "did" for a standard active statement is unnecessary and creates an interrogative or emphatic structure that is contextually inappropriate here.
 
• **Option 3: **"...which did Akbar the Great propounded." – Grammatically incorrect; the auxiliary "did" must be followed by the base form of the verb (propound), not the past tense.
 
• **Option 4: **"...had been a religion..." – Incorrectly changes the tense of the main clause from Simple Past to Past Perfect.

questions.question:
Arrange the parts to form a correct sentence:

(2) She poured it into a mug.
(3) She added tea leaves.
(4) She waited for it to brew.

• **Step 1:** The process begins with the action of boiling water, which is the starting point of making tea. Thus, **Sentence 1** is the first step.
 
• **Step 2:** After boiling water, it is poured into a mug. This makes **Sentence 2** the logical next step.
 
• **Step 3:** Once the water is in the mug, tea leaves are added to it. This makes **Sentence 3** the subsequent action.
 
• **Step 4:** Finally, the tea is left to brew, making **Sentence 4** the concluding action in the process.
 
• Thus, the correct sequence is **1-2-3-4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• When arranging sentences, it is important to identify the sequence of actions or events, ensuring that they follow a logical and chronological order.
 
• In this context, the process of making tea requires a clear progression: boiling water → pouring water → adding tea leaves → allowing it to brew.

 

**Arranged sequence:**

1. She boiled water.
2. She poured it into a mug.
3. She added tea leaves.
4. She waited for it to brew.

questions.question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate degree of comparison.

Madhu was the one who had eaten the ________ number of mangoes, only one!
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**3**' i.e. **least**.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
__
 
• The sentence uses a superlative degree of comparison to highlight that Madhu had eaten the smallest number of mangoes (only one).
 
• The superlative form of "less" is "least," which is used to describe the smallest amount or degree in comparison.
 
• The word "lesser" is incorrect in this context because it is a comparative form and not a superlative.
 
• The word "leastest" is grammatically incorrect and does not exist in English.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.
 
**Complete Sentence:** *"Madhu was the one who had eaten the **least**__ number of mangoes, only one!"*
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: "less"** is incorrect because it is not a superlative form.
 
• **Option 2: "lesser"** is incorrect because it is a comparative form, not a superlative.
 
• **Option 4: "leastest"** is incorrect because it is not a valid word in English.

questions.question:
Identify the error in the sentence.

She ran into the list to make sure she hadn't missed anything.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error is in **Option 3** ("into") due to the incorrect usage of a **phrasal verb**.
 
• The phrasal verb "**run into**" means to meet someone unexpectedly or to collide with something physically.
 
• The intended meaning here is to examine or review something quickly. The correct phrasal verb for this is "**run through**" or "**run over**."
 
• Since she is checking the items on a list, "**ran through**" is the grammatically and contextually appropriate choice.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"She **ran through** the list to make sure she hadn't missed anything."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1 ("ran"):** This is the correct past tense form of the verb "run," fitting the narrative sequence.
 
• **Option 2 ("missed"):** This is correctly used as the past participle in the past perfect construction ("hadn't missed"), indicating an action prior to the checking.
 
• **Option 4 ("list"):** This is the appropriate noun for a collection of items being checked.
 
• **Common 'Run' Phrasal Verbs:** 
 
 
• **Run out of:** To have no more of something.
 
• **Run away:** To escape from a place or situation.
 
• **Run after:** To chase someone or something.

S. advocates endurance
questions.solution:

__

• Following this, "through rational detachment" **(Q)** logically connects to the advocacy of endurance, explaining how it is achieved.
 
• **The next part,** "over desire," **(P)** builds on the idea of detachment by contrasting it with a negative concept that Stoic thought seeks to overcome.
 
• **Ending with** "and inner control" **(R)** completes the sentence by emphasizing the goal of inner strength and mastery.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option (2) SQPR.**

• **Option 3 (PSQR):** This option begins with "over desire Stoic thought advocates endurance," which is grammatically and contextually incorrect, as it places the contrast before introducing the main subject.
